extracted.intended_audience: political leaders, speechwriters, policymakers, and students of public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for crafting public political statements and symbolic messages that mobilize mass opinion and preserve coalition unity; covers timing, wording, structure, messenger selection, and organizational presentation of choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized timing and source for symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: “They are employed by somebody at a particular moment. The words must be spoken by people who are strategically placed, and they must be spoken at the opportune moment. Otherwise they are mere wind. The symbols must be earmarked.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure symbolic phrases are delivered by recognized, strategically placed authorities at moments when audiences are receptive; otherwise symbolic language will be ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols derive power from association
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is no power in the symbol, except that which it acquires by association in the human mind.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symbols that connect to pre-existing experiences, attachments, or authorities in the target audience so the phrase acquires real motivating force rather than remaining abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structure/numbering to convey precision and businesslike character
rubrics_metrics.description: “The numbering of them was an artifice to secure precision, and to create at once the impression that here was a business-like document.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize statements (e.g., numbered points) to give the impression of clarity, order and actionable policy — this helps attract attention and lends credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance inclusivity with constraint in public terms
rubrics_metrics.description: “They had to meet the national aspirations of each people, and yet to limit those aspirations so that no one nation would regard itself as a catspaw for another.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame terms broadly enough to satisfy various constituencies while inserting limits so no single partner feels used; aim to preserve coalition unity without promising incompatible outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft statements as viable alternatives to opponent negotiations
rubrics_metrics.description: “They were intended to compete for attention by substituting for the spectacle of Russo-German parleys the much grander spectacle of a public world-wide debate… they had also to be the terms of a possible peace.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make public proposals plausible and implementable so they can function as real alternatives to rival negotiations and persuade elements inside the adversary polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise phrasing to cover contingencies and signal meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: instead of saying Alsace-Lorraine should be 'restored' the Fourteen Points used 'righted' and referenced 'Prussia' and '1871' — wording chosen with meticulous care to satisfy multiple audiences and to signal specific boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words that are sufficiently ambiguous to accommodate different interpretations while including precise cues (dates, names) that signal intended boundaries to informed parties; this lets a phrase satisfy diverse expectations without committing to undesired particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke shared emotion through symbolic vagueness
rubrics_metrics.description: “They stood for opposing ideas, but they evoked a common emotion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use broadly resonant, somewhat vague phrases that different groups can project their private hopes onto; this creates emotional unity even when intellectual agreement is thin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade concreteness for inclusivity when raising the hierarchy of symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: “As you ascend the hierarchy in order to include more and more factions you may for a time preserve the emotional connection though you lose the intellectual… As you go up in the balloon you throw more and more concrete objects overboard.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that making symbols more universal increases reach but reduces specific meaning; choose the level of abstraction according to whether broad emotional mobilization or precise policy commitments are the priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit mass communication to create common consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: “Without cable, radio, telegraph, and daily press, the experiment of the Fourteen Points would have been impossible. It was an attempt to exploit the modern machinery of communication to start the return to a 'common consciousness' throughout the world.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use available mass media channels deliberately to synchronize attention and create a shared frame of reference across disparate publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame issues as concrete yes/no choices for mass decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: “The limit of direct action is for all practical purposes the power to say Yes or No on an issue presented to the mass.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing a mass audience, reduce complex matters to clear, binary or strongly focalized choices (or well-structured preferential options) so the public can register support or opposition; complexity must be reframed into actionable propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use organizational hierarchies to formulate and present choices
rubrics_metrics.description: “The essential fact remains that a small number of heads present a choice to a large group… the caucus, the nominating convention, and the steering committee [are means] of formulating a definite choice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on leadership structures (steering committees, caucuses) to translate diffuse private preferences into coherent public options that can be voted on or acted upon by a mass; mass action alone rarely constructs or administers complex solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select messengers recognizable as authoritative rather than merely expert
rubrics_metrics.description: “We choose between trustworthy and untrustworthy reporters… The people on whom we depend for contact with the outer world are those who seem to be running it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize messengers who are perceived as authoritative and connected to power or experience by the intended audience, since perceived authority often matters more than pure technical expertise in shaping public belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of choices determines effectiveness of voting systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Even complex ballots (e.g., preferential) depend on 'the quality of the choices presented' for the mass decision to be meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No voting method can substitute for poor options — invest effort in presenting clear, well-designed alternatives; the mechanism (referendum, preferential ballot) amplifies but does not fix the substance of choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing messages to moments of public receptivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Public receptivity shifts after events: e.g., the Christmas truce and Brest-Litovsk made people ask 'Why not?' and look east; these circumstances made the Fourteen Points salient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor events that alter public mood and deploy messages when audiences are naturally more open to alternative framings — timely proposals can capture attention and redirect debates.
